rv.q: I found it brilliantly, bizarrely funny, the sort of auteur performance that no other actor alive would so much as think of giving.
Smith-Cameron really is the heart and soul of this production, for all of Rylance's charisma.
Rylance's charisma knits together a production that's full of roustabout hilarity and poignancy mingled together, bright and bleak at once.

He sails dangerously close to giving a 'turn' instead of acting a part; his blustering innocent shtick and bent-kneed waddle of a walk is overdone, leaving the series of sucker punch revelations of the third act to land with too much of a discordant jolt.
In this enjoyable Gielgud staging, director Matthew Warchus, in particular, still doesn't seem to know quite what to make of Johnny Boyle, or how to handle his subplot.
But though the play has historic value and potent moments it feels hopelessly over the top in this staging.
But unfortunately it lands awry here, the contrasts more forced and awkward than illuminating.

While there are some hilarious set pieces and some compelling moments of pathos, the production never recovers from its uneven energy and slack pace. Mark Rylance provides a riveting focal point as alcoholic, tall-tale-telling ‘Captain’ Jack Boyle.
In this ultimately underwhelming production, one that's far too in thrall to its star casting, there is not enough room for such complexity.
He is tapping into the slurred vaudevillian razzmatazz he gave us in Jerusalem, but in his own silo.
His clowning goes so over the top that he might as well be auditioning for Mrs Brown's Boys.
In the event, the show is a Vaudevillian travesty of the tragi-comic tale of the titular Paycock.

It is easy to see from Matthew Warchus's compelling revival of Sean O'Casey's tragi-comic play Juno and the Paycock, about the cost of poverty and war on humanity, why it is called 'The Irish Masterpiece.'
Matthew Warchus's production negotiates the changes of mood to excellent effect, as when after terrified Johnny thinks he has seen a ghost they start singing Irish songs.
If not landing with the full force that it might, this staging still makes O'Casey's grimly resonant point about the futile horror of civil war and sectarian politics.
This is an unusual revival, giving both the comedy and tragedy full scope, but in the final scene it topples off balance into melodrama and becomes a different play altogether.
Poetic and poignant, this potentially great revival feels a little too uneven to soar.
Perhaps this hit-and-miss show has opened in the wrong capital. It would thrive in Dublin. London may lack the patience for it.

Despite the faithful attention to O'Casey's lines, this version of Juno and the Paycock is more a vehicle for the comedy talents of Rylance, and it's sure to please the legions of his fans. But O'Casey aficionados will likely be disappointed.
A tepid and sluggish show that took a long, long time to make the point that life is s**t and then you die.
Yet the result is a horrible melange. Everyone on stage seems to be performing in a different version of the play, there is no chemistry, little sense of purpose.
Mark Rylance is on irresistible form as Jack: a piercing tipsy stare beneath heavy black brows, his tiny moustache and striped pants sometimes seeming almost Charlie-Chaplin as he lurches around.
